questions.q: What is the tradeoff between Limited LOB mode and Full LOB mode?
options: Limited LOB mode only works for CDC, Full LOB mode only for full loads
Full LOB mode is always faster because it skips validation
Limited LOB mode is faster but truncates LOBs larger than a configured max; Full LOB mode handles any size but is slower since each LOB is fetched in a separate pass
There is no performance difference between the two
questions.explain: Limited LOB mode trades completeness for speed by capping size; Full LOB mode trades speed for completeness by fetching LOBs of any size in a separate pass.

questions.q: A migration task's full load finished quickly, but CDC latency keeps climbing instead of staying near zero. What's the most likely cause and general fix?
options: The target S3 bucket is in the wrong AWS region
LOB columns are never the cause of CDC latency, only full-load slowness
The source database has no transaction log — the fix is to enable one after CDC has already started
An undersized replication instance — the fix is a larger instance class or splitting the migration across multiple tasks
questions.explain: Growing CDC latency is a classic sizing symptom — the replication instance can't keep up with the rate of changes, and a larger instance class or splitting the workload usually resolves it.

questions.q: Why can a replication instance succeed at a full load but still fail during CDC?
options: Full loads don't require any network connectivity at all
CDC requires a persistent connection to the source's transaction log, which can fail even when short-lived connections (like a full load's queries) succeed
CDC failures are unrelated to networking in every case
CDC always runs on a completely different replication instance
questions.explain: A full load can complete over a connection that works for the duration of a query, while CDC needs the connection to stay open continuously — a difference that surfaces security-group timeouts and undersized VPN links that a full load never exercised.

questions.q: What does DMS's data validation feature compare?
options: Only the schema definitions, never the data itself
The CPU utilization of the source vs. target databases
The replication instance's own internal logs against CloudWatch
Row counts and, optionally, row-level content between the source and target tables after migration
questions.explain: Validation compares source and target data (row counts, and optionally row content) to catch mismatches from type conversion issues, collation differences, or timing gaps.

questions.q: Which of these is a common cause of DMS validation failures?
options: Running the migration task more than once
Using S3 instead of Redshift as a target
The replication instance being too large
Data type mismatches or collation/timezone differences between source and target engines
questions.explain: Validation failures often trace back to how values convert differently between engines — type mismatches, collation, or timezone handling — rather than to instance sizing.
